claims.text: Tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys are candidate materials for fusion plasma-facing or thermal-barrier applications.
The as-fabricated alloy contains coherent nanoprecipitates.
Irradiation dose produces increasing point-defect and defect-cluster accumulation in tungsten-based refractory HEAs.
Irradiation-induced defects modify dislocation mobility in tungsten-based refractory HEAs.
Irradiation-induced defects modify interactions between dislocations and nanoprecipitates during thermal cycling.
Irradiation defects disrupt conventional dislocation glide and climb and thereby enhance pinning or reduce mobility.
Thermal cycling around 1000°C activates dislocation motion.
Changes in defect-controlled dislocation mobility govern high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
Irradiated and thermally cycled samples will have lower dislocation mobility than the non-irradiated baseline.
Irradiation will reduce the nanoindentation plastic-zone size relative to the non-irradiated baseline.
Reduced dislocation mobility and a smaller plastic zone will produce changes in macroscopic plastic strain and toughness.
Nanoindentation can be used to assess irradiation-dependent plastic-zone size.
Some tungsten-containing refractory HEAs exhibit ductile mechanical behavior at 1000°C.
The proposed mechanism should hold around 1000°C at early-stage fusion-relevant irradiation doses and service-relevant strain rates.
Tungsten is susceptible to radiation-induced embrittlement.
Holding alloy composition and nanoprecipitate distribution constant while varying irradiation dose would isolate the irradiation effect.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to isolate irradiation, but the experimental samples receive irradiation plus thermal cycling whereas the control is described as thermally equilibrated or processed under standard thermal conditions rather than receiving an explicitly identical thermal-cycling history. Thus irradiation and thermal history may be confounded.
